title: Kestrel and the Compass
premise: Gideon Sterling, a mountain guide blacklisted from two countries, has survived five years by never taking the same route twice and never looking back at the wreck of the Kestrel, the salvage job that killed her father and got her name struck from every registry that matters. When her old rival Mara Voss hires her crew for a run to the same wreck — now stirring legal interest because a compass recovered from it points to a fortune the courts refuse to acknowledge belongs to anyone — Gideon refuses, until Voss reveals she's already sent Gideon's estranged half-sister down as advance diver. Racing a salvage fleet across six tides, Gideon must decide whether justice outside the law means claiming the inheritance or destroying it so no fleet can ever own what her father died protecting. She beats the fleet by one tide, but chooses to sink the treasure rather than let either side profit, walking away with something rarer: her sister, her crew, and a name she finally stops running from.
about_author: Tamsin Nystrom is a former deckhand on Arctic survey vessels who turned to writing after a storm off the Lofoten Islands left her with a broken wrist and too many stories. She lives in a converted lighthouse keeper's cottage in Norway, where she still climbs, dives, and keeps a brass compass on her desk that has never once pointed north.

chapters.title: The Long Way Down
chapters.summary: Gideon Sterling guides a wealthy client over a pass she's crossed eleven times, taking the dangerous route out of habit rather than need. POV: Gideon. The beat establishes her restlessness — she moves constantly because stopping lets the past catch up — and ends with a telegram waiting at the valley station bearing a name she hoped was dead: Voss.

chapters.title: Blacklisted
chapters.summary: Flashback woven through present-day drinking in a port town: how the Kestrel wreck job five years ago cost her father his life and her both licenses. POV: Gideon. Emotional beat: grief hardened into rules. She burns the telegram, but the bartender mentions strangers asking about 'the Sterling girl' — someone hasn't taken no for an answer.

chapters.title: An Offer With Teeth
chapters.summary: Mara Voss finds Gideon anyway, offering triple rates for a six-tide window to reach the Kestrel before the Halcyon salvage fleet files its claim. POV: Gideon. Beat: fury and temptation in equal measure. Gideon refuses flatly — until Voss slides over a photograph of the advance dive team, and Gideon recognizes her estranged half-sister, Wren.

chapters.title: The Crew That Shouldn't Exist
chapters.summary: Gideon assembles her old crew: engineer Okafor, navigator Pell, and diver Sefu, each carrying their own grudge against the registries that erased them. POV: rotating crew perspectives. Beat: wary reunion, old debts surfacing. They agree not for money but because none of them can stomach the fleet winning. The boat leaves on the morning tide.

chapters.title: Six Tides
chapters.summary: Open water. Voss lays out the timetable: the Halcyon fleet departs in six tides; whoever reaches the wreck first holds claim under maritime custom if not law. POV: Gideon. Beat: tension between Gideon and Voss, rivals forced into uneasy command. First sign of trouble — a fast cutter shadowing them at the horizon's edge.

chapters.title: The Cutter
chapters.summary: The shadowing vessel is Halcyon's scout ship, probing their course. Okafor rigs a decoy light pattern while Pell threads a fog bank. POV: Pell. Beat: competence under pressure, first blood of the race — they lose two hours but shake the scout. Gideon realizes the fleet knows their route, which means someone aboard is selling information.

chapters.title: Wren
chapters.summary: A radio burst reaches them: Wren's advance team went dark two tides early, off-schedule, off-contact. POV: Gideon. Beat: fear cracking open the anger she's carried since their father's funeral, when Wren chose the law-abiding path and Gideon chose exile. Gideon commits fully to the race — no longer for the wreck, but for her sister.

chapters.title: Storm Glass
chapters.summary: A squall line forces a choice: shelter and lose a tide, or run the reef channel at night. POV: Sefu. Beat: trust tested. They run it; the boat survives with a cracked hull plate and Okafor's hands bleeding. Sefu confesses he once took Halcyon money — not betrayal, just desperation years ago — deepening the paranoia about the leak.

chapters.title: Three Tides Out
chapters.summary: Halfway. Voss reveals why she really wants the wreck: the compass recovered from the Kestrel doesn't point north — it points to a ledger vault holding proof that Halcyon's founder stole the salvage rights from dozens of blacklisted crews, including Gideon's father. POV: Voss. Beat: the job transforms from treasure hunt to reckoning. Gideon doesn't know whether to believe her.

chapters.title: The Leak
chapters.summary: Pell catches a coded transmission leaving the boat. Suspicion falls on everyone; Gideon nearly throws Voss overboard before tracing the signal to a hidden relay Okafor built years ago and forgot to strip. POV: Okafor. Beat: relief curdling into shame — the crew's real enemy is their own accumulated secrets. One tide lost. Four remain.

chapters.title: The Shoals of Honest Men
chapters.summary: They cut through waters patrolled by a coastal authority that would love to arrest all of them. A bribe, a forged manifest, and Pell's flawless paperwork get them through — barely. POV: Pell. Beat: the theme lands — justice outside the law requires people willing to be criminals for the right reasons. Gideon starts drafting a plan that isn't about beating the fleet anymore.

chapters.title: Two Tides
chapters.summary: The Halcyon fleet appears on the horizon, a day ahead of schedule — the scout ship bought them more time than expected. Voss proposes scuttling the fleet's lead dredger; Gideon refuses to become what she's fleeing. POV: Gideon. Beat: moral crossroads. Instead they rig a false distress signal to pull the fleet toward a phantom wreck site, buying hours with deception instead of violence.

chapters.title: One Tide
chapters.summary: The gambit works but costs them their reserve fuel. They arrive at the Kestrel's coordinates with one tide of margin and no room for error. POV: Gideon. Beat: dread and focus. On the seafloor below, faint and wrong, a diver's emergency strobe blinks — Wren is alive, trapped in the wreck's flooded cargo deck, and the tide is turning against her.

chapters.title: Down
chapters.summary: Gideon dives herself, against every rule she's kept for five years, into the wreck that killed her father. POV: Gideon. Beat: terror transmuted into purpose. She finds Wren alive behind a jammed bulkhead, air running low, and the two sisters work the jam together — the first honest words between them in five years passing through hand signals and shared rope.

chapters.title: What the Compass Points To
chapters.summary: Freeing Wren, they find the compass itself mounted where their father left it, pointing into a sealed compartment: the ledger vault, intact, holding proof of Halcyon's thefts and the names of every crew defrauded. POV: Wren. Beat: inheritance redefined — not gold, but evidence, and the obligation that comes with it. The fleet's searchlights break the surface above.

chapters.title: The Fleet Arrives
chapters.summary: Halcyon's lead dredger anchors overhead; divers descend with legal papers and illegal intentions. Voss negotiates loudly on deck as a distraction while the crew seals the vault compartment and prepares to blow the wreck's remaining structure. POV: Voss. Beat: her redemption arc crystallizes — she's spent her career inside the law and found it rotten; this is her one act outside it.

chapters.title: Climax: Six Fathoms Down
chapters.summary: The demolition charge misfires as Halcyon divers breach the wreck. Gideon goes back down a third time, alone, to arm it manually while Wren and Sefu hold the line above against boarders. POV: Gideon. Beat: the climax — she stands in her father's drowned workspace, sets the charge beside the compass, and understands at last that letting go is not the same as losing.

chapters.title: The Kestrel Falls Silent
chapters.summary: The wreck collapses into the trench, burying the vault, the compass, and any claim Halcyon could ever file. The fleet withdraws to contest nothing. POV: multiple, braided. Beat: catharsis and cost — the explosion takes the last physical trace of Gideon's father, and she surfaces weeping into Wren's arms while the crew watches the fleet lights recede.

chapters.title: Aftermath, Above Water
chapters.summary: Voss copies the ledger pages she photographed during the negotiation ruse — enough to reopen the fraud cases for forty blacklisted crews — and gives them to a maritime journalist rather than the courts. POV: Voss. Beat: justice distributed sideways, outside the law's slow machinery. Gideon and Voss part without forgiveness but with respect, which is more than either expected.

chapters.title: Names Restored
chapters.summary: Weeks later, the fraud story breaks; registries begin reinstating names, Gideon's among them. She declines the license, preferring to work unregistered on her own terms. POV: Gideon. Beat: identity resolved — she was never the blacklist's creature; she was always free, she'd just believed otherwise. Wren asks to join the crew.

chapters.title: The Route Nobody Maps
chapters.summary: The refitted boat sails north with Gideon, Wren, Okafor, Pell, and Sefu aboard, no contract, no destination filed. POV: Gideon. Beat: quiet joy — movement chosen rather than imposed. Gideon opens her father's old logbook and reads the final entry for the first time: not coordinates, but a blessing. She finally stops moving away and starts moving toward.

chapters.title: Kestrel and the Compass
chapters.summary: Epilogue: a year on, the crew runs rescue missions for stranded divers and blacklisted sailors, funded by nothing and accountable to no registry. A young guide blacklisted like Gideon once was sends a desperate message; the crew alters course. POV: Gideon. Final beat: the compass on her chart table still doesn't point north — it points wherever someone needs pulling out of the water, and that, she decides, is north enough.
